k-1.x_notes: Strengths: six substantial, well-chosen problems with actual-size boards (1-inch edges). P1 mixes tileable shapes, odd-area shapes and an even-area but unbalanced shape (5 up/3 down). P2 has fewest-green triangles of sizes 2-4. P3 asks for all tilings of the unit hexagon (2) and the 2-1-1 hexagon (3). P4 asks for the fewest blocks. P5 is a good placement game: Dawson's-Kayles strips of 4/5/6/7 triangles (first/second/first/first) and a hexagon cycle (second player wins). P6 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon. The layout is clean. Weaknesses: there is no 'small blocks only' rule, although upscale blocks are in the room, and each P4 shape is exactly a 3x triangle, 2x rhombus or 2x trapezoid, so one big block would trivialize it. Only the pictured palette implies the restriction. P3 does not say which copies go with which shape. P6 asks kindergartners to draw six tilings on half-size hexagons, which is fiddly and less concrete, and it is inconsistent with P3, where they place blocks on copies.
k-1.y_notes: Same six problems, boards and mathematics as X, all correct and at actual size. Small improvements: the opening rule says 'Use only the small blocks', which matters because of the upscale blocks and P4's shapes. P3 separates the two shapes with a rule and says 'top shape... then the bottom shape'. P5 prints 1st/2nd in large bold that is easy to circle. P6 gives eight actual-size copies across two pages, so children build each tiling with blocks and compare them side by side, which is more concrete for K-1. Weaknesses: P6 needs many blue blocks (up to 48 per complete set) and leaves no drawn record. The page 7 'More copies' line is a small extra.
k-1.reason: The content is essentially identical. Y adds the needed small-blocks rule and makes P6 a hands-on build on actual-size copies instead of drawing on half-size grids, which suits kindergartners better.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a strong kernel-1 sequence with correct mathematics. P1: the star is balanced and has a forced tiling; the size-3 triangle has odd area; the 2-4 trapezoid has even area but 7 up/5 down; the 2-1-1 hexagon is tileable. P2 has holed boards (two up-holes impossible; one up and one down tileable) and a bowtie that is balanced but whose halves are unbalanced. P3 asks for fewest greens on triangles of sizes 2-5, plus a proof for the biggest. P5 compares chevrons with rhombi in a table. P6 asks children to design a 20-triangle board needing 6 greens (feasible with 13 up/7 down). P7 is the up/down rule for two greens on a side-2 hexagon; I checked all 144 up/down pairs work and no same-orientation pair does. Weaknesses: P3 runs onto an unlabeled page 4 holding only the size-5 triangle and lines. P4 is a thin 'imagine 10 and 100' question with three lines and no request to explain, short of a five-minute problem. P7 asks children to 'explain why your rule is right', which demands the sufficiency direction, beyond grade 2-3 proof. There is no small-blocks rule, although an upscale triangle or rhombus could muddle the green counts.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same boards and mathematics as X. Improvements: a small-blocks rule. P3 (sizes 2-4) and P4 (size-5 triangle, then 10 and 100, then 'explain why nobody can use fewer') make one coherent, substantial generalization-and-proof problem, with no unlabeled continuation page. P5 points back to P3 and P4 correctly. P7 asks children to explain why placements that break the rule can never work, which is the coloring argument they can actually give. Weaknesses: P3 alone is just filling three boxes, but it feeds P4. The rest is identical to X.
grades-2-3.reason: Both carry the same correct kernel-1 development. Y packages the size-5 triangle, the generalization and the proof into one real problem and words P7's proof demand appropriately, while X has an unlabeled continuation page and a thin P4.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a rich kernel-2 sequence. P1 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon. P2 introduces flips with a clear picture and names the move at once. P3 asks for shortest flip routes A to B, C to D and E to F on an actual-size side-2 hexagon. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip and whether 5 or 7 are possible. P5 is ribbons, with a correct LRRLR example. P6 is the parity proof and a lower bound for E to F. P7 counts all 20 tilings, and P8 counts the 20 tilings of the 1-3-3 hexagon. The ribbon definition is precise. Weaknesses: P2 makes children redraw all six coverings and then draw graph lines, which is busywork and directed scaffolding. P4 says 'start with any covering', but the two extreme 'cube' tilings have only one flippable hexagon, so a child who starts there (a natural choice) cannot make the required 4-flip loop. P4 also has only two lines and shares a page with P5. There is no small-blocks rule.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same boards, coverings A-F (pixel-identical) and mathematics as X. Improvements: a small-blocks rule. P2 is an open question that also asks 'how many moves'. P4 starts from covering A, which I checked has three flippable hexagons, two of them disjoint, so the 4-flip loop exists. P4 gives a five-hexagon strip to record each step, on its own page with room. P5 gets its own page. P7 allows 'draw or list', so children can list ribbons. Weaknesses: the move is not named 'flip' until P3, which is slightly awkward. P2 has a large unstructured blank area and no small boards. The ribbon wording ('from flat edge to flat edge') is a bit looser than X's.
grades-4-5.reason: The mathematics is the same. Y's P4 starts from a covering where the task is guaranteed to work and gives children a concrete recording strip, and Y avoids X's redraw busywork in P2, while X's only edges are earlier naming of 'flip' and a crisper ribbon definition.

overall.reason: The two packets are near-identical drafts with the same correct boards, problem sequences and kernel coverage, so either would run a good session. Y has small but consistent advantages in every band: an explicit small-blocks rule (relevant with upscale blocks present), a hands-on K-1 Problem 6, a coherent grade 2-3 generalization problem with an age-appropriate proof demand, and a well-posed, recordable grade 4-5 flip-loop task. X has no compensating advantages beyond minor wording.
